title: I committed to main by mistake
summary: The commit is on the wrong branch. What you do next depends entirely on whether it has been pushed.

steps.title: Find out whether the commit has left your machine
steps.look: The first line. 'ahead 1' means it is still local and you have easy options. If it is not ahead, it is already on the remote and rewriting is now other people's problem too.

signals.means: Still local. You can move it cleanly.
Already pushed. Do not rewrite shared history.

steps.title: Move the commit onto the branch it belonged on
steps.cmd: git branch {branch} && git reset --hard HEAD~1 && git switch {branch}
steps.note: reset --hard discards every uncommitted change in your working tree. Run git stash first if you have any. This is only safe because git branch {branch} was created on the line before, so the commit itself survives on that branch.
steps.look: After this, main is back where it was and your commit sits on {branch}.

signals.means: That branch already exists. Pick another name or switch to it and cherry-pick instead.

steps.title: Confirm nothing was lost
steps.look: Your commit on {branch}, and main matching the remote. If anything looks wrong, git reflog still has every prior position for about 90 days.

causes.cause: The commit exists only in your clone.
causes.fix: Create the branch at the current commit, then reset main back one. Nobody else is affected.

causes.cause: The commit is on the remote and others may have pulled it.
causes.fix: Do not reset and force-push. Use git revert to add a new commit that undoes it, then apply the original work on a proper branch.

causes.cause: A branch with that name is already present.
causes.fix: Switch to it and cherry-pick the commit across, then reset main.

verify: git log on main matches the remote's main.
Your commit appears in git log on {branch}.
git status reports a clean working tree, or exactly the changes you stashed.
escalate: Whether the commit was pushed, and whether anyone has pulled since

title: I need to force-push a rebased branch
summary: Rewriting a shared branch can silently destroy a colleague's commits. There is a safe form of this command.

steps.title: Check whether anyone else has pushed to this branch
steps.look: Commits you do not recognise. If someone else's work is on this branch, a force-push will delete it and they will not get a warning.

signals.means: Read the author of each. Anything not yours means stop and talk to them first.

steps.title: Force-push, but only if the remote is where you last saw it
steps.note: This rewrites remote history. --force-with-lease aborts if someone pushed since your last fetch, which plain --force does not. Never use plain --force on a shared branch. If this is a protected branch, it should be rejected by policy, not by your judgement.
steps.look: A forced update line. If it is rejected with 'stale info', someone pushed after your fetch and the lease did its job.

signals.means: The lease saved you. Someone pushed after your last fetch. Fetch again and re-examine before retrying.
Branch protection blocked it. That is working as intended; open a PR instead.

causes.cause: Other people have commits on this branch.
causes.fix: Do not force-push. Merge their work in, or coordinate a window with them first.

causes.cause: Someone pushed between your fetch and your push.
causes.fix: Fetch, inspect what arrived, rebase onto it, then retry with --force-with-lease.

causes.cause: Branch protection rules forbid force-push.
causes.fix: Open a pull request. If the rewrite is genuinely required, it needs a repo admin, not a workaround.

verify: {remote}/{branch} points at your intended commit.
No commits by other authors disappeared from the log.
CI on the branch is green after the rewrite.
escalate: git log --oneline of local and remote branch
The exact push output including any rejection reason
Whether the branch is protected and who owns it

title: Merge or rebase stopped with conflicts
summary: Git cannot combine two changes automatically and is waiting for you to decide.

steps.title: See exactly which files are unmerged
steps.look: Lines starting UU are both-modified. AA is both-added, DU and UD are delete-versus-modify, which need a decision rather than an edit.

signals.means: Both sides changed the same file. Edit it and resolve.
One side deleted what the other changed. Neither version is automatically right.

steps.title: Understand which operation you are inside
steps.look: Rebase and merge resolve identically but finish differently. Finishing the wrong way is where people lose work.

steps.title: See both sides of a conflicting file
steps.look: The conflict markers with both versions. The section above ======= is your current branch, below it is what you are bringing in.

steps.title: Abort and return to where you started
steps.look: A clean working tree back at the pre-merge commit. This is always safe for committed history, and is the right move when a merge has gone badly.
steps.note: Discards the entire in-progress merge and any conflict resolution you have done so far. Committed work is untouched, but unsaved resolution effort is lost. Inside a rebase, the equivalent is git rebase --abort.

causes.cause: Both branches changed the same lines.
causes.fix: Edit the file to the intended final state, remove the markers, git add it, then continue.

causes.cause: One branch deleted a file the other modified.
causes.fix: Decide deliberately: git rm to accept the deletion, or git add to keep the modified version.

causes.cause: Finished a rebase with git commit instead of git rebase --continue.
causes.fix: Inside a rebase always use git rebase --continue. Inside a merge, git commit is correct.

verify: git status reports a clean tree with no unmerged paths.
The build and tests pass on the merged result.
Neither side's intent was silently dropped.
escalate: Whether it is a merge or a rebase
Which files conflicted and how each was resolved

title: You are in detached HEAD state
summary: Commits made here belong to no branch and become unreachable when you switch away.

inputs.label: Branch to keep the work on

steps.title: Confirm the state and whether you have made commits
steps.look: 'HEAD detached at' confirms it. If the log shows commits you made here, they exist but nothing points at them yet.

signals.means: Detached. Any commits here need a branch before you move.

steps.title: Create a branch at your current position
steps.look: Your commits are now on a real branch and safe. Do this before anything else, and before switching away.

steps.title: If you already switched away and lost them, find them in reflog
steps.look: Every position HEAD has held, with its SHA. Detached commits remain here for about ninety days, so almost nothing is truly lost.

steps.title: Recover a specific lost commit
steps.look: A branch named recovered holding the work. Verify with git log before relying on it.
steps.note: Creates a new branch pointing at that commit. Nothing existing is modified and no history is rewritten, but pick the SHA carefully or you will branch from the wrong point.

causes.cause: HEAD points at a commit rather than a branch.
causes.fix: Create a branch here with git switch -c. Do it before switching away.

causes.cause: You left detached HEAD and the commits seem gone.
causes.fix: They are in the reflog. Find the SHA and branch from it.

causes.cause: You checked out a tag or old commit deliberately.
causes.fix: Fine as long as you make no commits. If you do, branch first.

verify: git status shows you on a named branch.
git log on that branch contains your commits.
The branch is pushed, or you know it is local only.
escalate: git reflog around the time the work was done

title: Push rejected for file size
summary: The remote refuses a file over its limit. Deleting it in a new commit does not help; it is still in history.

steps.title: Read the rejection and identify the file and commit
steps.look: The remote names the file and the commit that introduced it. That commit is what must change, not your latest one.

signals.means: Size limit. The file is embedded in history and must be removed from it.

steps.title: Find the largest objects actually in history
steps.cmd: git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check="%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)" | findstr blob
steps.look: Sizes are in bytes. This shows what is really in the repository, which is often not what you expected.

steps.title: If it is only in your last commit, remove it there
steps.look: git show --stat no longer lists the file. The file remains on disk because only the index entry was removed.
steps.note: Rewrites your most recent commit. Safe if that commit has not been pushed. If it has been pushed and others have pulled it, do not amend — the file needs removing from shared history through a coordinated rewrite instead.

causes.cause: The file is in an earlier commit, so deleting it now changes nothing.
causes.fix: It must be removed from history. For a single unpushed commit, amend. For anything shared, coordinate a rewrite with the repository owner.

causes.cause: The file is a legitimate large asset.
causes.fix: Track it with Git LFS and add the pattern to .gitattributes before committing it again.

causes.cause: A build artifact or database dump got committed.
causes.fix: Add it to .gitignore. Artifacts belong in a registry, not in Git.

verify: The push is accepted.
The repository size is reasonable for a fresh clone.
.gitignore or .gitattributes prevents a recurrence.
escalate: Whether that commit has been pushed and pulled by others

title: Commits show the wrong author or email
summary: Work commits attributed to a personal address, or the reverse. Usually a missing per-repository config.

steps.title: See what identity the recent commits carry
steps.look: The email is what matters for attribution on the hosting side. The display name is cosmetic.

steps.title: See which config is being used and from where
steps.cmd: git config --show-origin user.email && git config --show-origin user.name
steps.look: The file path in the output tells you whether this is global or repository-local. A missing local value means the global one applies.

steps.title: Set the correct identity for this repository only
steps.cmd: git config user.email "{email}" && git config user.name "{name}"
steps.look: git config --show-origin now points at the repository's own config file.
steps.note: Writes to .git/config for this repository only. Existing commits are unaffected — this changes future commits, nothing more. Setting it locally is the right move when you mix work and personal repositories on one machine.

steps.title: Fix the identity on the most recent commit
steps.look: git log shows the corrected author on the top commit.
steps.note: Rewrites the last commit, changing its SHA. Safe while unpushed. If it has been pushed, this creates a divergence that requires a force-push, which rewrites shared history.

causes.cause: No repository-local identity, so a global one applied.
causes.fix: Set user.email locally in each work repository. Consider clearing the global value so it can never apply silently.

causes.cause: The wrong-author commits are already on the remote.
causes.fix: Leave them. Rewriting shared history to fix a display name is not a worthwhile trade.

causes.cause: The email is right but commits show as unverified.
causes.fix: That is signing, not authorship. Set up commit signing separately.

verify: New commits carry the correct author.
git config --show-origin points at the local config.
No shared history was rewritten to achieve it.
escalate: Output of git config --show-origin for user.email
Whether the affected commits are pushed

title: Push rejected as non-fast-forward
summary: The remote has commits you do not have locally. Fetch and integrate before pushing.

steps.title: See how far the branches have diverged
steps.look: The ahead and behind counts. Behind only means a simple pull; both ahead and behind means real divergence that needs a decision.

signals.means: Only behind. A pull will fast-forward cleanly.
Diverged. You must choose merge or rebase.

steps.title: See exactly which commits are on each side
steps.look: Arrows point to which side each commit is on. Read the remote-side commits before deciding; someone else wrote them.

steps.title: Bring the remote work in beneath yours
steps.look: git status shows ahead only. Conflicts may pause the rebase; resolve then continue.
steps.note: Replays your local commits on top of the remote ones, which rewrites their SHAs. Safe for commits you have not pushed. If any of your local commits are already public elsewhere, use a merge instead so their identity does not change.

steps.title: Push once it is a fast-forward
steps.look: The push is accepted. If it is rejected again, someone pushed while you were rebasing; fetch and repeat.

causes.cause: You are only behind.
causes.fix: git pull. Nothing of yours is at risk.

causes.cause: Both sides have commits.
causes.fix: Rebase for a linear history, merge to preserve exact commit identity. Team convention decides.

causes.cause: Tempted to force-push past it.
causes.fix: Do not. Those remote commits are someone's work and force-push deletes them silently.

causes.cause: Pushing to a branch you did not intend.
causes.fix: Check git status -sb. The upstream may not be what you assume.

verify: The push is accepted.
git log shows both sets of commits.
Nothing from the remote disappeared.

title: Pull refuses because of local changes
summary: Git will not overwrite uncommitted work. It is protecting you, not blocking you.
aliases: your local changes would be overwritten

steps.title: See exactly what is uncommitted
steps.look: Which files are modified. Git names the conflicting ones in the error, and those are the only ones that matter.

signals.means: Untracked files. These only block if the incoming change adds the same path.
Modified tracked files that the pull would overwrite.

steps.title: Check whether the changes are worth keeping
steps.look: The actual content. Often this is debug output or a local config tweak you do not want anyway.

steps.title: Set the work aside and pull
steps.cmd: git stash push -m "before pull" && git pull
steps.look: The pull succeeds. Your changes are listed in git stash list.
steps.note: Moves your uncommitted changes onto the stash and restores a clean tree. The work is recoverable with git stash pop, but untracked files are not stashed by default and can still block the pull. Add -u if you need them included.

steps.title: Bring your work back on top
steps.look: Your changes reappear. Resolve any conflicts as with a normal merge.
steps.note: Reapplies the stashed changes and removes the entry from the stash. If it conflicts with what you just pulled, the entry is kept rather than dropped, so nothing is lost. Use git stash apply instead if you want to keep the entry regardless.

causes.cause: Tracked files differ from the incoming version.
causes.fix: Stash, pull, pop. Or commit them on a branch if they are real work.

causes.cause: An untracked file has the same path as an incoming one.
causes.fix: Move or delete yours. Git will not silently overwrite it.

causes.cause: The changes are local noise.
causes.fix: git checkout -- <file> discards them. Confirm with git diff first; this cannot be undone.

causes.cause: The changes are real work.
causes.fix: Commit them on a branch, then pull. The stash is for short-lived interruptions, not storage.

verify: The pull completes.
Your changes are back and intact.
The stash list is empty or intentionally populated.
escalate: The diff of the blocking files
Whether the work was stashed or discarded

title: Every file shows as modified with no real change
summary: git diff reports whole-file changes you did not make. Line ending conversion.

steps.title: Confirm the change is only line endings
steps.look: If the second command shows nothing, the difference is purely whitespace and line endings. That is definitive.

signals.means: Only line endings differ. No real content changed.

steps.title: Check the current conversion setting
steps.look: On Windows true converts to CRLF on checkout and back to LF on commit. A value of false or an inconsistent one across the team produces exactly this.

steps.title: Check what Git thinks each file should be
steps.look: What .gitattributes declares. Unspecified means Git guesses per machine, which is why it differs between teammates.

steps.title: Normalise the repository
steps.look: git status shows the normalised files staged. Commit them as a single dedicated change.
steps.note: Rewrites the index using the current .gitattributes rules, producing one large commit touching many files. Coordinate it with the team: anyone with in-flight branches will hit conflicts across every touched file. Commit it alone, with nothing else in the change.

causes.cause: core.autocrlf differs between machines.
causes.fix: Stop relying on it. Commit a .gitattributes file so behaviour is defined by the repository, not by each laptop.

causes.cause: No .gitattributes, so Git guesses.
causes.fix: Add one. At minimum * text=auto, with eol=lf pinned for shell scripts.

causes.cause: A shell script has CRLF and fails at runtime.
causes.fix: Pin *.sh text eol=lf. CRLF in a shebang produces exec format errors in containers.

causes.cause: The editor saves with different endings.
causes.fix: Configure it to respect .gitattributes. VS Code does by default.

verify: git status is clean after a fresh checkout.
Shell scripts run in containers.
.gitattributes is committed so it applies to everyone.
escalate: The core.autocrlf value and its origin

title: gitignore is ignored for a file
summary: You added a pattern but Git keeps tracking the file.

steps.title: Ask Git which rule applies
steps.look: The file and line of the matching rule. No output means no rule matches, which is a pattern problem rather than a caching one.

signals.means: A rule does match. If the file is still tracked, the cache is the reason.
No rule matches this path.

steps.title: Check whether the file is already tracked
steps.look: gitignore only affects untracked files. Once a file is tracked, no pattern will ever make Git stop following it.

steps.title: Check for a negation rule later in the file
steps.look: Rules are applied in order and a later negation wins. Also note that a directory excluded by an earlier rule cannot have its contents re-included.

steps.title: Stop tracking it without deleting it
steps.look: git status shows the deletion staged and the file no longer tracked. Commit, and it will then be ignored.
steps.note: Removes the file from Git's index while leaving it on disk. On the next pull, anyone else's checkout will have this file deleted from their working tree, so tell the team. If it holds secrets, removing it now does not remove it from history.

causes.cause: The file is already tracked.
causes.fix: git rm --cached, then commit. gitignore has no effect on tracked files.

causes.cause: No rule matches the path.
causes.fix: Check for a leading slash, which anchors to the repository root. Patterns are relative to the .gitignore file's own location.

causes.cause: A later rule re-includes it.
causes.fix: Rules apply in order. Reorder them.

causes.cause: A parent directory is excluded.
causes.fix: Git does not descend into excluded directories, so a negation inside one never applies. Unexclude the directory first.

causes.cause: The file contains secrets and was committed.
causes.fix: Ignoring it now does not remove it from history. Rotate the secret; treat it as leaked.

verify: git status no longer lists the file.
check-ignore names the intended rule.
Any leaked secret has been rotated.

title: I deleted a branch that had work on it
summary: The branch is gone but the commits almost certainly still exist.

steps.title: Find the branch's last position in the reflog
steps.look: Deletion is recorded with the SHA the branch pointed at. That SHA is everything you need.

signals.means: The commit is recorded. Recovery is straightforward.
Nothing in this clone's reflog. It may have been deleted elsewhere.

steps.title: Check whether the commits are unreachable but present
steps.look: Dangling commits still in the object store. This finds work the reflog missed, such as after a clone or a reflog expiry.

steps.title: Look at a candidate before acting on it
steps.look: Confirm it is the right work. Branching from the wrong SHA wastes time and creates confusion.

steps.title: Recreate the branch at that commit
steps.look: The branch exists again, pointing at the same commit. Nothing else is modified. Verify with git log before continuing.

causes.cause: The commit is in the reflog.
causes.fix: git branch <name> <sha>. Reflog entries last about ninety days by default.

causes.cause: Not in this clone's reflog.
causes.fix: Check the remote, or another teammate's clone. Reflogs are strictly local and are not shared.

causes.cause: The branch existed on the remote.
causes.fix: git fetch origin <branch>:<branch> restores it directly. Far simpler than reflog archaeology.

causes.cause: Garbage collection removed the objects.
causes.fix: If fsck finds nothing and no remote has it, the work is gone. This is rare within the reflog window.

verify: The branch exists with the expected commits.
git log matches what you remember.
It is pushed so it cannot be lost locally again.
escalate: Whether the branch was ever pushed

title: Submodule directory is empty after clone
summary: The folder exists but contains nothing. Submodules are not fetched by default.

steps.title: Check the submodule's recorded state
steps.look: A leading minus means not initialised. A plus means it is at a different commit than the parent records. A space means it is correct.

signals.means: Not initialised. Nothing has been fetched.
Checked out at a different commit than the parent expects.

steps.title: Initialise and fetch everything
steps.look: Populates every submodule at the commit the parent records. Recursive matters when submodules contain their own.

steps.title: Check the submodule URL is reachable
steps.look: An SSH URL fails in CI that only has HTTPS credentials. This is a very common cause of submodules working locally and not in a pipeline.

steps.title: Check the parent records a commit that still exists
steps.look: The recorded SHA. If that commit was force-pushed away in the submodule repository, the checkout can never succeed.

causes.cause: Submodules were not fetched on clone.
causes.fix: git submodule update --init --recursive, or clone with --recurse-submodules.

causes.cause: The submodule is at a different commit.
causes.fix: update restores the recorded one. If you intended the new commit, commit that pointer in the parent.

causes.cause: The submodule URL cannot be reached.
causes.fix: Use a URL scheme the environment can authenticate to. Add an insteadOf rule for CI.

causes.cause: The recorded commit no longer exists upstream.
causes.fix: Someone force-pushed the submodule repository. Update the parent to a commit that exists.

causes.cause: CI does not fetch submodules.
causes.fix: Enable submodules in the checkout step. Most CI systems skip them by default.

verify: The submodule directory has content.
git submodule status shows no prefix.
A fresh clone works in CI, not only locally.
escalate: Whether it works in CI as well as locally

title: Git keeps asking for credentials
summary: Every push or pull prompts, or an old credential is reused and rejected.
aliases: support for password authentication was removed

steps.title: Check the remote URL scheme
steps.look: HTTPS uses a token through a credential helper. SSH uses a key. Which one you have determines everything that follows.

signals.means: HTTPS. A personal access token is needed; passwords no longer work.
SSH. The key is the credential.

steps.title: Check which credential helper is configured
steps.look: On Windows this should be manager. No helper means Git cannot store anything and will prompt every time.

steps.title: Check what is cached for the host
steps.look: Stored Windows credentials. A stale entry with an expired token is reused silently and produces repeated failures.

steps.title: Remove the stale credential
steps.look: The next push prompts once, then stores the new credential and stops asking.
steps.note: Deletes the stored credential for that host from Windows Credential Manager. The next Git operation will prompt for a fresh one, so have the new token ready. Other tools using the same stored credential will also start prompting.

causes.cause: HTTPS with a password.
causes.fix: Password authentication was removed. Use a personal access token as the password.

causes.cause: An expired token is cached.
causes.fix: Delete it from Credential Manager. Git will not overwrite it on its own.

causes.cause: No credential helper.
causes.fix: git config --global credential.helper manager.

causes.cause: SSH key is not loaded or not authorised.
causes.fix: Follow the SSH runbook. Test with ssh -T git@github.com.

causes.cause: Cached credentials belong to another account.
causes.fix: Common with work and personal accounts. Clear the entry and use the right one.

causes.cause: The token lacks repo scope.
causes.fix: Regenerate with the right scopes. Read-only tokens fail on push with a confusing message.

verify: Push and pull work without prompting.
The stored credential is for the right account.
The token has an expiry you know about.

title: I lost a stash
summary: A stash was dropped, popped into a conflict, or cleared. The content usually still exists.

steps.title: Check what stashes remain
steps.look: Empty means they were dropped or cleared. Stash entries are commits, and dropping one only removes the reference.

signals.means: Stashes exist. Check whether the one you want is among them.
No stashes listed. Look for dangling commits.

steps.title: Find dangling stash commits
steps.look: Unreachable commits still in the object store. A stash creates a merge commit, which is a strong identifying signal.

steps.title: Inspect a candidate before acting
steps.look: Confirm it is your work. A stash commit shows the working tree state at the time it was created.

steps.title: Restore it as a branch
steps.look: Creates a branch at that commit so it can never be garbage collected. Nothing else is modified.

causes.cause: The stash was dropped.
causes.fix: Find the commit in fsck output and branch from it. git stash drop prints the SHA; scroll back in the terminal.

causes.cause: A pop conflicted and the entry was kept.
causes.fix: Check git stash list. Pop keeps the entry when it conflicts, precisely so nothing is lost.

causes.cause: git stash clear was run.
causes.fix: The commits become unreachable but remain until garbage collection. fsck finds them.

causes.cause: The stash is in a different clone.
causes.fix: Stashes are local and are never pushed. Check other clones.

causes.cause: Garbage collection removed them.
causes.fix: If fsck finds nothing, they are gone. This is why stashes are for hours, not weeks.

verify: The work is on a branch.
git log shows the expected content.
It is committed properly rather than stashed again.
escalate: What git show reveals for each candidate

title: Git operations are very slow
summary: status, checkout and commit take many seconds in a repository that should be fast.

steps.title: Measure where the time goes
steps.look: size-pack and the loose object count. Many loose objects or a very large pack both slow everything down.

signals.means: Tens of thousands of loose objects. Repacking will help substantially.
A multi-gigabyte pack. Large binaries are likely in history.

steps.title: Find the largest objects in history
steps.cmd: git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check="%(objectsize) %(rest)" | sort -rn | head -10
steps.look: Sizes in bytes with paths. Binaries committed years ago still cost every clone, forever.

steps.title: Check the working tree size
steps.look: A very large working tree makes status slow regardless of history. Untracked build output is a common cause.

steps.title: Repack the repository
steps.look: count-objects shows far fewer loose objects and a smaller total.
steps.note: Repacks objects and permanently deletes anything unreachable, including reflog entries beyond the expiry and dropped stashes. If you are also trying to recover lost work, do that first — this removes exactly the objects fsck would have found. It can take a long time on a large repository.

causes.cause: Many loose objects.
causes.fix: git gc packs them. Routine maintenance usually handles it automatically.

causes.cause: Large binaries in history.
causes.fix: They cost every clone forever. Removing them requires a coordinated history rewrite.

causes.cause: Many untracked files slow status.
causes.fix: Add build output to .gitignore. Git scans everything otherwise.

causes.cause: Status scans the whole tree every time.
causes.fix: Enable core.fsmonitor on a large repository.

causes.cause: Antivirus scans every file Git touches.
causes.fix: Exclude the repository directory. On Windows this is frequently the dominant cost.

causes.cause: Large assets are tracked directly.
causes.fix: Move them to Git LFS going forward.

verify: Common operations feel fast.
Loose object count is low.
Large binaries are in LFS or excluded.

title: Cherry-pick stops with a conflict
summary: A commit does not apply cleanly to this branch because its context differs.

steps.title: See which files conflicted
steps.look: UU entries are conflicts. Cherry-pick applies a diff, so it fails whenever surrounding context differs from the original branch.

signals.means: Content conflict. Resolve as with a merge.
The file does not exist here in the same form.

steps.title: Look at what the original commit changed
steps.look: The intended change. Resolving well means reproducing that intent here, not just making the markers go away.

steps.title: Check whether the change is already present
steps.look: A commit with the same subject already on this branch means it was backported and the pick is unnecessary.

steps.title: Abort and return to a clean state
steps.look: A clean working tree at the pre-pick commit.
steps.note: Discards the in-progress cherry-pick along with any conflict resolution you have done. Committed history is untouched, but unsaved resolution work is lost. Use --skip instead if you want to abandon only this commit in a multi-commit pick.

causes.cause: The surrounding code differs from the source branch.
causes.fix: Resolve to the intended final state. Read the original commit to understand the intent.

causes.cause: The file does not exist on this branch.
causes.fix: The change may need adapting rather than picking. Consider whether it applies at all.

causes.cause: The change is already here.
causes.fix: Skip it. git cherry-pick --skip moves on in a multi-commit pick.

causes.cause: The commit depends on an earlier one not present.
causes.fix: Pick the dependency first, or pick the range.

causes.cause: You are picking many commits.
causes.fix: A merge or rebase is usually better than a long sequence of cherry-picks.

verify: The cherry-pick completes.
The change works on this branch, not just compiles.
Tests pass.
escalate: Whether the change is already present

title: I did my work on the wrong branch
summary: Changes are on main or another branch and need moving, committed or not.

steps.title: Check whether the work is committed
steps.look: Uncommitted changes move trivially. Committed ones need the branch pointer moved instead.

signals.means: Uncommitted. Switching branches carries them across.
Committed but not pushed. Move the commits.

steps.title: For uncommitted work, just switch
steps.look: Uncommitted changes follow you to the new branch. Nothing is lost and no history changes.

steps.title: For committed work, create the branch here first
steps.look: The branch now points at your commits. They are safe regardless of what you do to the original branch next.

steps.title: Reset the original branch back
steps.look: The current branch matches the remote. Your work is on {branch}.
steps.note: Discards every commit and every uncommitted change on the current branch beyond origin/main. This is only safe because the previous step created {branch} at the current commit, so the work survives there. Run git log {branch} and confirm your commits are listed before running this.

causes.cause: The work is not committed.
causes.fix: git switch -c carries it across. Simplest case.

causes.cause: Committed but not pushed.
causes.fix: Branch here, then reset the original. Nothing is shared yet so nothing breaks.

causes.cause: The commits are on the remote.
causes.fix: Do not reset and force-push a shared branch. Use git revert on the original and apply the work properly on a branch.

causes.cause: Only some changes belong on the branch.
causes.fix: Use git stash push with specific paths, or commit selectively with git add -p.

verify: The work is on the intended branch.
The original branch matches its remote.
Nothing shared was rewritten.

title: I need to undo a merge
summary: A merge introduced a problem and must be reversed. Merges revert differently from ordinary commits.
aliases: commit is a merge but no -m option

steps.title: Confirm it is a merge and find its parents
steps.look: Two parent hashes means a merge. Reverting one requires saying which side to keep, and that is what -m specifies.

signals.means: A merge commit with two parents. Reverting needs -m.

steps.title: Check whether it has been pushed
steps.look: Any remote branch listed means others may have it. That rules out rewriting history and points at revert instead.

steps.title: Revert keeping the first parent
steps.look: A new revert commit. The merged changes are gone from the working tree.
steps.note: Creates a new commit undoing the merged changes. History is not rewritten, which makes this safe for shared branches. Be aware that re-merging the same branch later will not reintroduce those changes, because Git considers them already merged — you must revert the revert first.

steps.title: Confirm the result
steps.look: The revert commit on top and a clean tree. Run the tests; a reverted merge can leave a half-consistent state if other work depended on it.

causes.cause: Reverting a merge needs -m.
causes.fix: -m 1 keeps the branch you merged into, which is what you want almost always.

causes.cause: The merge is local only.
causes.fix: git reset --hard to the commit before it is cleaner than a revert. No history is shared yet.

causes.cause: You reverted and now cannot re-merge.
causes.fix: Revert the revert. Git sees the branch as already merged otherwise.

causes.cause: Reverted with the wrong -m value.
causes.fix: Revert that revert and redo with the correct parent.

causes.cause: Later commits depend on the merged code.
causes.fix: Reverting will break them. Fix forward instead.

verify: The problem is gone.
Tests pass.
The path to re-merging later is understood.
escalate: Whether it is on any remote

title: Something broke and I do not know which commit did it
summary: A bug appeared somewhere in a range of commits. Bisect finds it in a handful of steps.

steps.title: Confirm the endpoints really are good and bad
steps.look: How many commits are in the range. Bisect needs about log2 of that many tests, so even hundreds of commits take under ten steps.

steps.title: Start the bisect
steps.look: Git reports roughly how many steps remain and checks out a middle commit.
steps.note: Checks out a commit partway through the range, leaving you in detached HEAD. Any uncommitted work is in the way and should be committed or stashed first. git bisect reset returns you to where you started.

steps.title: Test and mark each checkout
steps.look: Use good or bad after testing each one. Git halves the range each time and tells you how many steps are left.

steps.title: Return to where you started
steps.look: You are back on your original branch with a clean tree.
steps.note: Leaves bisect mode and restores your original branch. Do this when finished, or the repository stays in detached HEAD and subsequent commits will not belong to any branch.

causes.cause: Bisect names the first bad commit.
causes.fix: Read that commit. It is usually obvious once you know which one it is.

causes.cause: The test is not deterministic.
causes.fix: Bisect needs a reliable signal. Make the check deterministic first or the result is meaningless.

causes.cause: Some commits cannot be built or tested.
causes.fix: git bisect skip. Git works around them.

causes.cause: Testing by hand is slow.
causes.fix: git bisect run <script>. An exit code of zero means good, non-zero means bad.

causes.cause: The good commit is not actually good.
causes.fix: The result will be wrong. Verify both endpoints before starting.

verify: The first bad commit is identified.
The repository is out of bisect mode.
The cause is understood, not just located.
escalate: How the good and bad endpoints were verified
The test used at each step

title: A rebase went wrong and I want out
summary: Mid-rebase, conflicts everywhere, or the result looks nothing like what was intended.

steps.title: Check whether a rebase is in progress
steps.look: Whether you are mid-rebase. That determines whether you abort or undo a finished one.

signals.means: Still mid-rebase. Abort returns you cleanly.
No rebase in progress. A finished rebase is undone through the reflog.

steps.title: Abort an in-progress rebase
steps.look: Returns to exactly where you started. Nothing committed is lost, only the conflict resolution you had done.

steps.title: For a finished rebase, find where you were
steps.look: The entry just before the rebase started, usually marked rebase (start). That SHA is your pre-rebase state.

steps.title: Reset back to the pre-rebase commit
steps.look: git log matches what you had before the rebase.
steps.note: Discards the rebased commits and any uncommitted changes, returning the branch to its pre-rebase state. The rebased commits remain in the reflog for about ninety days, so this is recoverable, but anything uncommitted right now is not. Verify the SHA with git show before running it.

causes.cause: A rebase is in progress.
causes.fix: git rebase --abort. Clean and complete.

causes.cause: The rebase completed and the result is wrong.
causes.fix: Find the pre-rebase SHA in the reflog and reset to it.

causes.cause: Every commit conflicts.
causes.fix: You are probably rebasing onto the wrong base. Check the target branch.

causes.cause: The branch was rebased after being pushed.
causes.fix: Everyone who pulled now has divergent history. Coordinate before force-pushing.

causes.cause: Rebasing a long-lived branch.
causes.fix: Merge instead. Rebase suits short private branches.

verify: The branch is in the state you intended.
git status is clean.
No shared history was rewritten without agreement.
escalate: Whether a rebase is in progress
What the branch looked like before
